title: Gatekeepers and Hallucinations: A Layered Evaluation Framework for LLM-Driven Quantum Circuit Generation
authors: Christopher Coleman, Sharon Marfatia
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become embedded in quantum simulation workflows (IDE copilots, notebook assistants, agentic pipelines), evaluation must move beyond functional correctness to anticipate and catch structured failures before they propagate through expensive pipelines. We present a layered evaluation framework for materials-informed Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) circuit generation: (i) a gatekeeper screening rubric across seven physical and framework criteria; (ii) a circuit fidelity analysis comparing model outputs against analytical and reference-implementation values for H2/STO-3G/Jordan-Wigner/UCCSD, with ansatz classification and gate-composition breakdown; and (iii) design entropy, a run-to-run behavioral consistency metric. We surface a taxonomy of five distinct LLM failure modes (geometry hallucination, nonexistent API usage, runtime integration failures, constraint violations, and plausible-but-unverifiable output), each with distinct detectability profiles and structural to the task rather than to any one model. A forensic audit of the evaluation platform's own source code further establishes that two apparent model failures originated in the harness through silent fallback-template substitution, demonstrating that evaluation infrastructure belongs inside the same trust boundary as the models it tests. Applied across multiple foundation models on a Materials Project integrated pipeline, the framework shows that gatekeeper-style validation is necessary, not optional, for reliable deployment.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated quantum circuits need layered validation because failures can be structurally plausible yet physically or operationally invalid.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For quantum software pipelines, gatekeeper checks and consistency metrics can prevent costly downstream errors in VQE circuit generation and similar workflow automation.
method: Screen outputs with seven physical/framework gatekeeper criteria.
Compare generated H2/STO-3G/Jordan-Wigner/UCCSD circuits against analytical and reference implementations.
Measure design entropy to assess run-to-run consistency and classify failure modes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across multiple foundation models, the framework identified five distinct failure modes and also traced two apparent model errors to silent fallback behavior in the evaluation harness.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation infrastructure itself must be treated as part of the trust boundary, since harness bugs can mimic model failures and distort conclusions.
infographic.paper_title: Gatekeepers and Hallucinations: A Layered Evaluation Framework for LLM-Driven Quantum Circuit Generation

title: Separation of Statistical Complexity and Trainability in Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Suman Mandal, Maximillian Daughtry, Eduardo R. Mucciolo
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are among the leading approaches for near-term quantum computing, yet their performance can degrade in barren plateau regimes characterized by vanishing gradients. A widely held intuition is that increasing circuit expressivity, often associated with random-state behavior, leads to a loss of trainability. Existing results show that sufficiently random circuits can lead to barren plateaus. Here we show that standard statistical signatures of randomness can emerge well before this regime, without degrading trainability. We demonstrate this behavior in structured variational circuits applied to the one-dimensional cluster-Ising model and a generalized toric code Hamiltonian. To characterize state complexity, we analyze Porter-Thomas statistics, entanglement-spectrum level statistics, and inverse participation ratios. Across both models, increasing circuit depth drives these diagnostics toward random-state-like or random-matrix-like behavior, while variational optimization remains effective, with no evidence of exponential gradient suppression in the regime studied. We interpret this behavior in terms of locality. Spectral correlations develop at relatively shallow depth through locally generated structure, while global state randomization and the associated concentration-of-measure effects are not yet realized. These results show that commonly used statistical diagnostics of complexity do not by themselves determine trainability. Instead, they point to a separation between different aspects of complexity in finite-depth variational circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Statistical signs of randomness can appear in variational quantum circuits well before trainability is lost, so complexity and barren-plateau behavior are not the same thing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For NISQ circuit design, deeper or more expressive ansätze may still optimize well even when they look random by common complexity diagnostics, so trainability must be checked directly.
method: Studied structured VQAs on the 1D cluster-Ising model and a generalized toric code Hamiltonian.
Measured complexity with Porter-Thomas statistics, entanglement-spectrum level statistics, and inverse participation ratios.
Compared these diagnostics against variational optimization performance as circuit depth increased.
infographic.evidence_signal: As depth increased, the circuits moved toward random-state-like or random-matrix-like signatures while optimization remained effective and showed no exponential gradient suppression in the studied regime.
infographic.watch_item: The result is depth- and model-dependent: these diagnostics may indicate higher complexity without guaranteeing that the circuit will still avoid barren plateaus at larger scales.
infographic.paper_title: Separation of Statistical Complexity and Trainability in Variational Quantum Circuits

title: Towards an Optimally Distributed Quantum Fourier Transform Circuit
authors: Zachary Vernec, Michael Silver, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
abstract: A promising avenue for scaling quantum computing is to connect quantum processing units (QPUs) by generating entanglement between them. This requires circuit partitioning: partially rewriting quantum circuits to run on a distributed quantum system using quantum teleportation protocols, while preserving the unitary operation implemented by the circuit. The key metric to minimize when partitioning is the e-bit count, defined as the number of maximally entangled qubit pairs that must be generated between QPUs. We focus on partitioning the quantum Fourier transform (QFT) circuit, which is widely used as a subroutine in quantum algorithms such as quantum phase estimation and arithmetic circuits. Specifically, we present a partitioning scheme based on optimal gate-packing, compare it against prior analytical partitioning schemes for the QFT, and evaluate it against partitions produced by general-purpose circuit partitioning algorithms. We further validate our approach by implementing the partitioned circuit on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that an optimal gate-packing strategy can partition the Quantum Fourier Transform into a distributed circuit while reducing the entanglement cost measured by e-bit count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves how QFT-based workloads can be mapped onto multi-QPU quantum hardware, making distributed quantum execution more practical and scalable.
method: Derive a QFT partitioning scheme using optimal gate-packing.
Compare the scheme against prior analytical QFT partitioning methods.
Benchmark against general-purpose circuit partitioners and validate on quantum hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparative evaluation of the proposed partitioning method against prior approaches and general-purpose algorithms, plus hardware implementation of the partitioned circuit.
infographic.watch_item: Results may depend on hardware connectivity, teleportation overhead, and the fidelity required to preserve the target unitary across QPUs.
infographic.paper_title: Towards an Optimally Distributed Quantum Fourier Transform Circuit

title: Quantum Chip Paradigm Framework
authors: Cai, Ling Qiao, Bin Yang, Fumin Luo, WeiGui Guo, GuoRong Zhang
abstract: Quantum Electronic Design Automation (Q-EDA) is emerging as quantum chips move from laboratory prototypes to scalable engineering systems. This paper argues that superconducting quantum chip design is approaching a "SPICE moment" similar to early classical EDA, where growing qubit scale, control complexity, frequency planning, packaging, process variation, and cryogenic measurement feedback require a shift from experience-based design to model-driven engineering. We propose a Quantum Chip Paradigm Framework that treats Q-EDA not only as software, but as part of the quantum chip development paradigm. Unlike classical HDL-first design, quantum chip design must begin with physical structures such as Josephson junctions, resonators, couplers, readout elements, control lines, and packaging environments. The framework emphasizes PCell-based modeling, SPICE-Q simulation, Quantum PDKs, and design-technology-measurement co-optimization. We further outline a hierarchical Q-EDA system spanning physical structures, qubit PCells, logical qubits, quantum arithmetic, functional quantum IP, and Quantum SoC systems. The key goal is to turn physical models, layout rules, simulation results, fabrication data, and measurement feedback into reusable and auditable engineering objects for large-scale quantum processors and fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a Quantum Chip Paradigm Framework that shifts superconducting quantum chip design from experience-based practice to model-driven Q-EDA using physical, reusable engineering abstractions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It matters because scaling quantum processors will require integrated workflows for layout, simulation, packaging, fabrication, and cryogenic measurement feedback, much like classical EDA transformed chip design.
method: Use PCell-based representations for Josephson junctions, resonators, couplers, readout elements, control lines, and packaging.
Adopt SPICE-Q, Quantum PDKs, and design-technology-measurement co-optimization.
Organize Q-EDA hierarchically from physical structures to qubit PCells, logical qubits, quantum arithmetic, IP, and Quantum SoC systems.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract is a conceptual framework paper and does not report new experimental results or quantitative benchmark data.
infographic.watch_item: A major implementation challenge is standardizing accurate device, process, and measurement models across fabrication and cryogenic test environments.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Chip Paradigm Framework

title: Preparation of Fractional Quantum Hall States on Quantum Computers
authors: Hao Wu, Lei-Yi-Nan Liu, Zhao-Xin Pei, Yi-Xuan Zhai, Zhen-Xu Luo, Zhao Liu
abstract: The realization of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, characterized by fractional charge and intrinsic topological order, on quantum computers represents a central challenge at the interface of condensed matter physics and quantum information science. Current methods are grouped into two types: methods based on (quasi-)adiabatic evolution of complex parent Hamiltonians to yield target states, and circuit-based approaches for direct state preparation, which are confined to effectively one-dimensional systems near the thin cylinder or torus limit. We introduce a complementary scheme relying on direct quantum circuit construction, which works for arbitrary geometries. Specifically, we present a method to precisely prepare the $ν=1/3$ Laughlin state on the sphere geometry and demonstrate that it significantly reduces the required number of two-qubit gates and circuit depth, compared to variational quantum circuit approaches. In addition, we employ optimal control techniques to design control pulses for both superconducting and Rydberg atom platforms, identifying experimentally feasible protocols for state preparation. Our results provide an efficient and hardware-relevant pathway for realizing generic FQH states on both noisy intermediate-scale and fault-tolerant quantum devices.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a direct quantum-circuit method to prepare the ν=1/3 Laughlin fractional quantum Hall state on arbitrary geometries, including the sphere, with lower gate count and depth than variational approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a more hardware-friendly route to implementing topologically ordered quantum states on near-term superconducting and Rydberg platforms, as well as on future fault-tolerant devices.
method: Construct direct quantum circuits for exact state preparation rather than relying on (quasi-)adiabatic evolution.
Specialize the approach to the sphere geometry to efficiently prepare the ν=1/3 Laughlin state.
Use optimal control to translate the circuit idea into experimentally feasible pulses for superconducting and Rydberg hardware.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the proposed scheme significantly reduces two-qubit gate count and circuit depth compared with variational quantum circuit methods and identifies feasible control protocols on two hardware platforms.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is still a specialized state-preparation protocol and its practical performance may depend strongly on hardware fidelity and the complexity of scaling to larger target systems.
infographic.paper_title: Preparation of Fractional Quantum Hall States on Quantum Computers

title: Scalable quantum circuit knitting using a weak-coupling approximation
authors: John P. T. Stenger, Daniel Gunlycke, Nikos Chrisochoides
abstract: We present a method for performing distributed quantum computing with controlled approximations. Exact distributed quantum computing requires exponential classical information to reconstruct the quantum process. However, we show how the classical cost is reduced to polynomial if the quantum procedure can be partitioned between a qubit that is weakly coupled the other qubits. We demonstrate our method for a layered circuit based on the circuits used for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that distributed quantum computing can be made scalable by using a weak-coupling approximation, reducing classical reconstruction cost from exponential to polynomial when a circuit can be partitioned around weakly coupled qubits.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables practical quantum circuit knitting for larger problems by lowering the classical overhead of distributed execution, especially for layered variational circuits such as those used in QAOA.
method: Partition the quantum procedure across a qubit weakly coupled to the rest of the circuit.
Use a controlled approximation to reconstruct the global process with polynomial classical cost.
Demonstrate the approach on layered QAOA-like circuits.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a demonstration on a layered circuit based on QAOA circuits, showing the method on a representative benchmark family.
infographic.watch_item: The approximation depends on a weak-coupling assumption, so accuracy and applicability may degrade when inter-qubit coupling is strong or the partition is not natural.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable quantum circuit knitting using a weak-coupling approximation

title: Reconstruction of detector error model for quantum error correction
authors: Cheng Ye, Pan Zhang
abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing fundamentally relies on the accurate characterization of circuit-level noise to optimize decoding algorithms. However, extracting complex multi-body error correlations remains challenging. Contemporary greedy inference algorithms can suffer from statistical distortion, discarding true physical mechanisms while introducing many unphysical false positives. Here, we introduce the Correlation-Analysis-based Hypergraph Reconstruction (CAHR) algorithm, a globally consistent framework to invert experimental syndrome statistics directly into discrete physical hypergraphs. By coupling exact algebraic correlation equations with a top-down concurrent-pruning strategy, CAHR recovers the fault topology without false positives for both $d=5$ rotated surface codes and dense 8-body 2D color codes in our benchmark settings. Furthermore, we show that exact continuous parameter extraction in dense codes is limited by a \textit{variance cascade}, where absolute statistical variance accumulates linearly from high- to low-degree mechanisms. This motivates a two-stage inference paradigm: utilizing CAHR to extract the fault topology, followed by continuous probability optimization. This provides a practical approach for characterizing and decoding highly correlated noise in realistic quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: CAHR reconstructs discrete detector error hypergraphs from syndrome data using exact correlation equations and concurrent pruning, avoiding the false positives common in greedy inference.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a practical two-stage workflow for quantum hardware characterization: first recover fault topology, then optimize error probabilities for more reliable decoding.
method: Invert syndrome statistics with exact algebraic correlation equations.
Use a top-down concurrent-pruning strategy to eliminate unphysical error mechanisms.
Separate topology recovery from continuous probability fitting in dense correlated codes.
infographic.evidence_signal: In benchmark tests on d=5 rotated surface codes and dense 8-body 2D color codes, CAHR recovered the fault topology without false positives.
infographic.watch_item: Exact continuous parameter extraction can still be limited by variance cascade in dense codes, so probability estimates may degrade even when topology is correct.
infographic.paper_title: Reconstruction of detector error model for quantum error correction

title: Nonequilibrium steady states induced by stochastic mid-circuit measurements and resets on a quantum computer
authors: Jakob Murauer, Sabine Tornow, Gabriele Perfetto
abstract: Stochastic resetting has emerged as a versatile protocol to drive quantum many-body systems to non-equilibrium steady states by interspersing unitary dynamics with measurements and resets at random times. In spite of this, a quantum hardware validation of such non-equilibrium steady states is still missing. Here, we achieve this goal by first formulating a noisy discrete-time theory where unitary gates alternate with noisy mid-circuit projective measurements and conditional resets. This noisy conditional resetting theory is then demonstrated on a superconducting quantum processor for up to $N=7$ qubits. We consider, as a paradigmatic case, the unitary dynamics of the interacting Floquet transverse-field Ising model. The stationary state of the noisy conditional resetting agrees quantitatively with the experiments, and it shows crossover behavior related to the equilibrium quantum phase transition of the model. Our results might thus pave the way for the preparation of collective stationary states on noisy quantum devices and for further developments of quantum algorithms involving mid-circuit measurements.

infographic.key_insight: Stochastic mid-circuit measurements and resets can drive a noisy quantum processor into reproducible non-equilibrium steady states, and those steady states can be modeled quantitatively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a hardware-valid protocol for preparing and studying collective stationary states on near-term superconducting quantum devices, with direct relevance to mid-circuit measurement-based algorithms.
method: Built a noisy discrete-time theory with unitary gates alternating with noisy mid-circuit projective measurements and conditional resets.
Implemented the protocol on a superconducting quantum processor for up to 7 qubits.
Used the interacting Floquet transverse-field Ising model as the benchmark dynamical system.
infographic.evidence_signal: The stationary state predicted by the noisy conditional-resetting theory matches the experimental results quantitatively and shows crossover behavior tied to the model’s equilibrium quantum phase transition.
infographic.watch_item: The results are demonstrated only up to 7 qubits and depend on realistic noise in mid-circuit measurement/reset operations, so scaling and error sensitivity remain key concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Nonequilibrium steady states induced by stochastic mid-circuit measurements and resets on a quantum computer

title: Exceptional-Point-Anchored Variational Quantum Eigensolver for Non-Hermitian Many-Body Phase Diagrams: Bridging Skin-Effect Topology and Entanglement Criticality on NISQ Hardware
authors: Akoramurthy B, Surendiran B, Xiaochun Cheng
abstract: We introduce the Biorthogonal Variational Quantum Eigensolver (B-VQE), a quantum algorithm for simulating non-Hermitian many-body systems on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. Non-Hermitian quantum matter exhibits exceptional points, parity-time symmetry breaking, and non-Hermitian skin effects, yet existing quantum algorithms often rely on costly post-selection procedures and are not designed to capture biorthogonal eigenstates. B-VQE employs independent variational circuits to represent the left and right eigenstates of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian and optimizes a biorthogonal objective function that directly tracks non-Hermitian phase transitions. The framework incorporates an Exceptional-Point Detector (EPD) that identifies exceptional points through a hardware-native coalescence metric and a Non-Hermitian Quantum Geometric Tensor (NH-QGT) readout that distinguishes state-topological and band-topological signatures in interacting many-body systems. To overcome the exponential overhead associated with conventional non-Hermitian simulation, we develop an importance-sampling mitigation strategy that removes the need for ancilla-based post-selection while retaining polynomial computational scaling. We validate the approach on three representative models: a non-Hermitian Hubbard chain, a non-Hermitian XXZ spin chain, and a two-dimensional non-Hermitian (t)-(J) model. B-VQE achieves relative energy errors below (5\times10^{-3}) and locates exceptional points with high accuracy on noise-free simulations while resolving phase boundaries associated with localization, quantum scars, and skin-effect physics. These results establish B-VQE as a scalable NISQ methodology for constructing non-Hermitian many-body phase diagrams and exploring topological and critical phenomena in open quantum systems.

infographic.key_insight: B-VQE extends variational quantum eigensolvers to non-Hermitian many-body systems by using separate left/right circuits and a biorthogonal objective to detect exceptional points and phase transitions directly on NISQ hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a hardware-friendly route to map non-Hermitian phase diagrams without ancilla-heavy post-selection, making open-system and skin-effect physics more tractable on near-term quantum devices.
method: Uses independent variational circuits for left and right eigenstates of a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian.
Optimizes a biorthogonal loss with an Exceptional-Point Detector to locate eigenstate coalescence.
Adds NH-QGT readout and importance-sampling mitigation to reduce overhead and capture topological/critical signatures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on three benchmark models, with relative energy errors below 5×10^-3 on noise-free simulations and accurate exceptional-point localization.
infographic.watch_item: Results are reported primarily in noise-free simulation, so performance under realistic NISQ noise and scaling to larger interacting systems remains to be demonstrated.
infographic.paper_title: Exceptional-Point-Anchored Variational Quantum Eigensolver for Non-Hermitian Many-Body Phase Diagrams: Bridging Skin-Effect Topology and Entanglement Criticality on NISQ Hardware

title: SPICE-Q and Large-Scale Quantum Chip Production
authors: Cai, Ling Qiao, Bin Yang, Fumin Luo, Chang Liu, WeiGui Guo
abstract: We propose SPICE-Q, a SPICE-inspired design-technology co-optimization framework for superconducting quantum processors. Rather than replacing tools such as HFSS, Qiskit Metal, pyEPR, SQcircuit, SQuADDS, scqubits, or QuTiP, SPICE-Q aims to connect them through a unified, traceable data chain spanning process rules, layout, electromagnetic simulation, energy-participation-ratio and circuit quantization, Hamiltonian extraction, noise analysis, cryogenic test, and manufacturing feedback. The central mapping is from process and PDK constraints to layout geometry, electromagnetic modes, equivalent circuit parameters, effective Hamiltonians, and finally metrics such as frequency, coupling, anharmonicity, decoherence, readout performance, and yield. This flow must capture Josephson-junction variability, transmon frequency allocation, resonator and Purcell constraints, coupler crosstalk, microwave routing, 3D interconnects, material/interface loss, package modes, and wafer-scale process statistics. By introducing standardized model interfaces, statistical parameter models, model cards, version governance, and closed-loop calibration from cryogenic and fabrication data, SPICE-Q frames superconducting quantum-chip design as an engineering workflow rather than a collection of isolated simulations. We argue that scalable and fault-tolerant quantum processors will require such a continuous model chain from device physics and electromagnetic fields to quantum dynamics, noise, manufacturability, and system-level yield.

infographic.key_insight: SPICE-Q is a SPICE-like co-optimization framework that links superconducting qubit design stages into one traceable pipeline from process rules to quantum performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It gives quantum hardware teams a practical workflow for integrating layout, EM simulation, circuit quantization, noise analysis, fabrication, and cryogenic test to improve scalability and yield.
method: Unifies existing tools (HFSS, Qiskit Metal, pyEPR, SQcircuit, SQuADDS, scqubits, QuTiP) through standardized interfaces.
Maps process/PDK constraints to geometry, EM modes, circuit parameters, Hamiltonians, and device metrics.
Adds statistical parameter models, model cards, version governance, and closed-loop calibration from fab and cryogenic data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract is a framework proposal and synthesis of the design-to-test workflow, not a results paper with reported experimental benchmarks or quantitative evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: A major implementation challenge is ensuring consistent models and data exchange across heterogeneous tools while capturing junction variability, parasitics, and wafer-scale process statistics accurately.
infographic.paper_title: SPICE-Q and Large-Scale Quantum Chip Production

title: Quantum Algorithm for Open-System Battery Cathodes by Modeling Multiple Strongly Coupled Holstein Polarons with Chain-Mapped Caldeira-Leggett Dynamics
authors: Joshua M. Courtney
abstract: Cathode lithiation occupies a chemical regime of tightly localized orbitals, narrow bandwidths, and strong electron-lattice coupling. The defining electrochemical observables (open-circuit voltage and differential capacity) are open-system, reservoir-equilibration quantities that closed-Hamiltonian quantum simulation cannot produce, set by exchange with electron, Li$^+$, and phonon baths. We present a fault-tolerant quantum algorithm that recovers them through a unitary chain-mapped Caldeira-Leggett embedding, rendering the baths Trotterizable. The resulting fourth-order Trotter step has a T-gate count polynomial in system size, validating its open-system dynamics against hierarchical equations of motion (HEOM) at strong coupling and the Lindblad limit at weak coupling. For single-carrier olivine LiFePO$_4$, a single voltage anchor on an otherwise DFT-fixed Hamiltonian places the differential-capacity peak within the $\pm5$ mV reproducibility of the experimental plateau. For multi-carrier spinel LiMn$_2$O$_4$, whose $1{:}1$ Mn$^{3+}$/Mn$^{4+}$ filling makes the inter-site Coulomb repulsion dynamically active, the same kernel yields a two-plateau voltage curve with a $125$ mV split, within $17\%$ of the observed $150$ mV. We deliver an end-to-end fault-tolerant resource estimate for such a multi-carrier, three-reservoir observable: $368$ logical qubits and $\sim3\times10^5$ T-gates per step, or $\sim1.7\times10^{12}$ T-gates for a full voltage curve (parallelizable over $\sim10^3$ trajectories), leaving the production-scale dynamical run as a milestone for future hardware. The same kernel reproduces macroscopic quantum coherence, two-band superconductivity, and the Mikheyev-Smirnov-Wolfenstein resonance without modification, placing dynamical battery chemistry and similar Hamiltonians within scope for fault-tolerant quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: A fault-tolerant quantum algorithm can simulate open-system battery cathodes by embedding electron, Li+, and phonon baths into a unitary chain-mapped Caldeira-Leggett model, enabling voltage and capacity predictions that closed-system methods cannot produce.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a path toward quantum simulation of real battery cathodes with chemically relevant strong coupling and reservoir equilibration, potentially informing cathode design and voltage-curve prediction.
method: Chain-map the baths into a unitary, Trotterizable Hamiltonian
Use a fourth-order Trotter step with polynomial T-gate scaling
Validate against HEOM at strong coupling and Lindblad dynamics at weak coupling
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with experiments for LiFePO4 within ±5 mV and LiMn2O4 within 17% of the observed 150 mV plateau split, plus a resource estimate of 368 logical qubits and about 3×10^5 T-gates per step.
infographic.watch_item: The resource requirements are still very large, and the full voltage-curve run is described as a future milestone rather than a demonstrated hardware-scale result.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Algorithm for Open-System Battery Cathodes by Modeling Multiple Strongly Coupled Holstein Polarons with Chain-Mapped Caldeira-Leggett Dynamics

title: Split-Head Quantum Generative Adversarial Network for Crystalline Material Discovery
authors: Huan-Ming Chang, Jen-Yu Chang, Tsung-Wei Huang, En-Jui Kuo
abstract: The discovery of novel crystalline materials is a critical challenge in computational materials science, often limited by the spatial representation limitations and mode collapse typical of classical generative models. Traditionally, developing Quantum GANs for continuous 3D space is hindered by the limited capacity of near-term hardware. To overcome this, we adapt a physics-informed "split-head" architecture right from the quantum trunk to explicitly decouple macroscopic lattice bounds from microscopic atomic coordinates, significantly maximizing resource efficiency. This study disentangles the contributions of quantum circuits from these architectural priors by evaluating a Split-Head Quantum Generative Adversarial Network against an architecture-matched classical ablation model. Evaluated on the highly constrained Mg-Mn-O system, the results reveal a highly nuanced performance dichotomy between the advanced models. The architecture-matched classical ablation model demonstrated superior thermodynamic precision. Conversely, the integration of quantum circuits in the SH-QGAN drove unparalleled structural breadth and latent space exploration, more than doubling the ablation's geometric validity and successfully generating novel, metastable candidates converging on the Mg2MnO4 stoichiometry. These findings clarify that while architectural separation of cell and atom generation drives strict thermodynamic precision, quantum feature mapping independently provides the spatial diversity necessary to overcome mode collapse. Both mechanisms offer distinct, complementary enhancements for the generative discovery of advanced materials.

infographic.key_insight: A split-head quantum GAN separates lattice-scale and atom-scale generation, and the quantum component mainly boosts structural diversity while the classical ablation is better at thermodynamic precision.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This architecture suggests a resource-efficient route for crystalline materials discovery on near-term hardware by combining physics-informed priors with quantum feature mapping.
method: Quantum trunk feeds a split-head generator that decouples cell bounds from atomic coordinates.
Compared SH-QGAN against an architecture-matched classical ablation to isolate the effect of quantum circuits.
Tested on the constrained Mg-Mn-O materials system to probe validity, novelty, and stoichiometric convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Mg-Mn-O, the classical ablation achieved better thermodynamic precision, while SH-QGAN more than doubled geometric validity and produced novel metastable candidates near Mg2MnO4.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the chosen architectural priors and the limited evaluation system, so gains may not directly transfer to broader crystal chemistries or larger-scale 3D generation.
infographic.paper_title: Split-Head Quantum Generative Adversarial Network for Crystalline Material Discovery

title: Quantum simulation of neutrino oscillations with bosonic encoding
authors: Sandeep Joshi
abstract: Superconducting qubits offer a versatile platform for quantum simulation. In this architecture, quantum information can be encoded in the bosonic modes of a microwave cavity, offering an alternative to conventional qubit-based encoding schemes. These cavity bosonic modes can be manipulated using a single ancillary qubit. In this work, we investigate the quantum simulation of two- and three-flavor neutrino oscillations using Fock-basis encoding of a cavity mode. We design pulse sequences for implementing the required unitary operations through selective number-dependent arbitrary phase (SNAP) and displacement gates. Pulse-level control is employed to realize high-fidelity gate operations on the encoded cavity mode. The resulting neutrino oscillation probabilities obtained from quantum simulation exhibit close agreement with the corresponding theoretical predictions, demonstrating the feasibility of cavity-based bosonic encoding schemes for quantum simulation.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that neutrino oscillations can be efficiently simulated on superconducting hardware by encoding the neutrino states in a cavity’s bosonic Fock modes and controlling them with a single ancilla qubit.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This demonstrates a hardware-friendly alternative to qubit-only encodings for quantum simulation, leveraging SNAP and displacement pulses for high-fidelity cavity control.
method: Encode two- and three-flavor neutrino states in the Fock basis of a microwave cavity mode
Implement the required unitaries with selective number-dependent arbitrary phase (SNAP) and displacement gates
Use pulse-level control with a single ancillary qubit to drive and read out the bosonic simulation
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulated neutrino oscillation probabilities closely match theoretical predictions, indicating successful gate implementation and model fidelity.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on precise pulse calibration and cavity control, so scaling and sensitivity to hardware errors may limit practical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum simulation of neutrino oscillations with bosonic encoding

title: MAPS: A Novel Multi-Axial Projective Sphere for Geometrically Visualizing Higher d-Valued Quantum State-Space of Qudits
authors: Ali Al-Bayaty
abstract: Visualizing the d-valued quantum state-space of quantum systems serves as a foundational pillar for the scientific research and practical applications in quantum computing and information science, where d >= 2. The 2-valued quantum states of a qubit are elegantly visualized on the three-dimensional Bloch sphere. In contrast, expanding this geometrical paradigm to visualize higher d-valued quantum states of a qudit (d >= 3), e.g., a qutrit (d=3), ququadit (d=4), and quintit (d=5), leads to severe structural and topological complexities. This paper introduces a new generalized three-dimensional framework to effectively visualize higher d-valued quantum states of a qudit, in the aspects of ease of illustration, structural simplicity, and natural representation for researchers and engineers. We called this new framework the "multi-axial projective sphere (MAPS)", which consists of n projectional intersecting spatial axes, where 0 <= n <= d-1. We also propose a group of novel d-valued phase axial-based gates, to swivel and shift d-valued quantum states of a qudit along these n axes. Our generalized framework could be used for visualizing high-dimensional data for practical applications, e.g., machine learning, quantum machine learning, and quantum chemistry, where every axis of the MAPS represents a single feature of such data with its corresponding distinct values.

infographic.key_insight: MAPS generalizes the Bloch-sphere idea to a 3D, multi-axis visualization framework for higher-dimensional qudit states (d≥3), aiming to make their geometry easier to interpret.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help engineers visualize and reason about multi-valued quantum states and high-dimensional features in quantum machine learning, quantum computing, and quantum chemistry.
method: Defines a multi-axial projective sphere (MAPS) with n intersecting spatial axes, where 0 ≤ n ≤ d-1.
Uses phase axial-based gates to swivel and shift qudit states along the MAPS axes.
Frames each axis as a distinct feature/value dimension for visualizing higher-dimensional data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract is conceptual and proposes a visualization framework; it does not report quantitative experiments, benchmarks, or evaluation results.
infographic.watch_item: The paper’s practicality may depend on how well the proposed 3D projection preserves true high-dimensional quantum-state structure without introducing misleading geometric simplifications.
infographic.paper_title: MAPS: A Novel Multi-Axial Projective Sphere for Geometrically Visualizing Higher d-Valued Quantum State-Space of Qudits

title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver-Based Quantum Bootstrap Embedding for Molecules
authors: Derek Peng
abstract: Simulating strongly correlated molecular systems on near-term quantum hardware remains challenging due to modern hardware's limited quantum volume and moderate-fidelity qubits. One potential way to circumvent this challenge is through bootstrap embedding (BE). Bootstrap embedding breaks molecules into smaller fragments that are then embedded into the "bath" of other fragments in an iterative way. Bootstrap embedding is appealing for quantum simulation because fragmenting the system reduces the qubit requirements for any given fragment. In this work, we develop a quantum bootstrap embedding (QBE) workflow that uses variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) fragment solvers and study the algorithmic choices that determine the overall VQE-QBE algorithm's success. To improve efficiency, we introduce FastAdaptVQE, a sparse matrix-accelerated form of the adaptive variational quantum eigensolver (ADAPT-VQE) that replaces symbolic commutator evaluation with direct statevector linear algebra, and MatrixFreeAdaptVQE, a matrix-free extension that removes the sparse-matrix memory bottleneck that appears when treating larger fragments. We also modify the ADAPT-VQE operator selection step by replacing the purely greedy choice with a look-ahead strategy. Benchmarks on $H_4$ and $F_2$ reach chemical accuracy, within 1 kcal/mol of bootstrap embedding results using a full configuration interaction (FCI) solver. These results show that combining QBE with VQE can accurately calculate energies of molecular systems. This research lays the foundation for extending energy calculations to larger molecular systems and quantum materials on near-term quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: The paper shows that variational quantum eigensolvers can be used as fragment solvers inside quantum bootstrap embedding to accurately simulate correlated molecules on near-term hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a practical path to reduce qubit requirements and improve scalability for molecular quantum simulation on noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices.
method: Split the molecule into fragments and embed each fragment in a self-consistent bath via bootstrap embedding.
Use VQE-based fragment solvers, with FastAdaptVQE and MatrixFreeAdaptVQE accelerating ADAPT-VQE operator selection and memory usage.
Replace greedy operator choice with a look-ahead strategy to improve convergence and robustness.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on H4 and F2 reached chemical accuracy, within 1 kcal/mol of bootstrap embedding results obtained with a full configuration interaction solver.
infographic.watch_item: Performance still depends on fragment size, operator-selection strategy, and the statevector/sparse-linear-algebra overhead needed for larger fragments.
infographic.paper_title: Variational Quantum Eigensolver-Based Quantum Bootstrap Embedding for Molecules

title: Matrix Product Operators In The Age of Block Encoding
authors: Eugene Dumitrescu
abstract: We develop a block-encoding compiler that speeds up linear combination of unitaries Hamiltonian simulation programs by treating matrix product operators as compressed, virtual-path LCU programs. In showing how these new conditional PREP and SELECT stages are compiled in terms of a parent matrix product operator, we go beyond typical operator splitting product formulas and illustrate how tensor networks are a natural language and valid intermediate representation for quantum circuits. Our results are numerically verified for two important cases, namely, Heisenberg and perturbed Heisenberg-adjacent chain real-time evolution, and highlight polynomial speedups. Specifically, we highlight a polynomial speedup that avoids the $\mathcal{O}(N^K)$ Pauli-string growth when the compressed MPO bond dimension and path normalization remain mild. We quantify how MPO truncation error and bond-dimension budgets affect the compiled polynomial representation. Our algorithms show how classical pre-processing in terms of tensor network data structures opens new avenues to accelerate quantum algorithms.

infographic.key_insight: Matrix product operators can act as a compressed intermediate representation for block-encoded Hamiltonian simulation, reducing the usual explosion in Pauli-string terms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a practical compiler-style path to faster quantum simulation pipelines by shifting work into classical tensor-network preprocessing and lowering resource growth when MPO compression is effective.
method: Treat MPOs as virtual-path LCU programs for Hamiltonian simulation.
Compile conditional PREP and SELECT stages from a parent MPO representation.
Use tensor-network compression and truncation to control bond dimension and polynomial size.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical verification on Heisenberg and perturbed Heisenberg-adjacent chain real-time evolution, with observed polynomial speedups.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on keeping MPO bond dimension and truncation error small; if compression quality degrades, the promised savings may weaken.
infographic.paper_title: Matrix Product Operators In The Age of Block Encoding

title: Piezoelectric resonators in thin-film barium titanate from room temperature to millikelvin
authors: Hao Tian, Shu-Yuan Chang, Nuha Akhtar, Kasra Sardashti, Mohammad Mirhosseini
abstract: Ferroelectric materials, with their strong nonlinearities, underpin key technologies across radio-frequency (RF) signal processing, optical communications, and emerging quantum systems. Barium titanate (BTO) is a notable example, combining strong piezoelectric and electro-optic responses. While bulk BTO has been studied for decades, the piezoelectric properties of its recently available thin films, and their behavior at the millikelvin temperatures relevant to quantum hardware, remain largely unexplored. Here, we fabricate and characterize surface acoustic wave (SAW) resonators on thin-film BTO. The measured devices exhibit high electromechanical coupling (k2eff 0.14 at 5.2 GHz) and operate up to 7.8 GHz. From these measurements, combined with finite-element modeling of the multi-domain microstructure, we extract an effective piezoelectric coefficient d33eff of 53 pC/N, comparable to bulk BTO. Exploiting the intrinsic ferroelectricity, we further demonstrate low-voltage switching with a fast (100 ns) response, attractive for reconfigurable RF front-ends and parametric amplifiers. Extending these measurements to millikelvin temperatures, we find that the piezoelectric response persists, with d33eff 19 pC/N, pointing to the potential of BTO for piezoelectric coupling in superconducting quantum circuits. These results position thin-film BTO as a promising piezoelectric platform for both classical and quantum information technologies.

infographic.key_insight: Thin-film barium titanate (BTO) retains strong piezoelectricity from room temperature down to millikelvin, enabling high-frequency resonators with potential quantum-hardware utility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The material offers a tunable piezoelectric platform for reconfigurable RF components and superconducting quantum circuits, with strong electromechanical coupling at microwave frequencies.
method: Fabricated SAW resonators on thin-film BTO
Measured electromechanical response from room temperature to millikelvin
Used finite-element modeling of the multi-domain microstructure to extract effective piezoelectric coefficients
infographic.evidence_signal: Devices showed k²eff = 0.14 at 5.2 GHz, operation up to 7.8 GHz, room-temperature d33eff = 53 pC/N, and millikelvin d33eff = 19 pC/N; switching occurred in 100 ns.
infographic.watch_item: Multi-domain microstructure and cryogenic integration may affect reproducibility, calibration, and device performance in scalable quantum hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Piezoelectric resonators in thin-film barium titanate from room temperature to millikelvin

title: Pulse-optimised circuit elements for scalable and noise-resilient quantum chemistry
authors: Henrik Gothen, Christopher K. Long, Djamila Hiller, Yunming Qian, Crispin H. W. Barnes, Normann Mertig
abstract: Useful chemistry calculations on near-term quantum processors are hindered by current algorithmic runtimes. We develop a methodology to significantly reduce these runtimes. Typically, variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithms are implemented as sequences of primitive gates. Our methodology instead relies on gradient-ascent pulse engineering to construct hardware-tailored pulses for the direct implementation of VQEs. As problem sizes increase, it quickly becomes intractable to optimise a pulse that implements an entire VQE ansatz circuit. However, leading VQEs are constructed in a modular fashion. A problem-tailored VQE is assembled from parameterised circuit elements that simulate hopping between two or four electronic spin orbitals. We show that these circuit elements can be implemented more efficiently using hardware-tailored pulses. We numerically demonstrate our methodology on a silicon spin-qubit quantum processor. We find that common circuit elements, known as single- and double-qubit excitations, can be implemented in less than 289 ns and 927 ns, respectively. Compared with conventional gate-based implementations, our pulse-accelerated qubit excitations provide a scalable approach for faster and therefore more noise-robust quantum chemistry simulations by reducing VQE runtimes by up to a factor of 15.3.

infographic.key_insight: Hardware-tailored control pulses can replace gate sequences for modular VQE circuit elements, dramatically cutting runtime while preserving chemistry functionality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster, more noise-resilient quantum chemistry on near-term devices by reducing the time qubits must remain coherent during VQE execution.
method: Use gradient-ascent pulse engineering to optimize pulses directly for the target hardware.
Implement modular VQE building blocks such as single- and double-qubit excitation circuits with tailored pulses.
Assemble larger chemistry ansätze from these optimized pulse-based elements instead of primitive gates.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a silicon spin-qubit processor, the authors report single- and double-qubit excitations executed in under 289 ns and 927 ns, with VQE runtime reductions of up to 15.3× versus gate-based implementations.
infographic.watch_item: Optimizing whole VQE ansätze as a single pulse becomes intractable at larger problem sizes, so scalability depends on how well the modular pulse elements compose across circuits and hardware settings.
infographic.paper_title: Pulse-optimised circuit elements for scalable and noise-resilient quantum chemistry

title: How Many Shots Are Enough for a Quantum Circuit?
authors: Giuseppe Bisicchia, Alessandro Bocci, Ernesto Pimentel, Antonio Brogi
abstract: Quantum algorithms require repeated circuit executions, known as shots, to estimate output distributions accurately. Determining the minimal number of shots needed to meet a target accuracy is crucial to reduce costs and resource usage, especially on today's noisy and expensive quantum hardware. In this paper, we address the shot optimisation problem in a black-box setting, where no assumptions are made about the structure of the quantum circuit or the noise model of the backend. We introduce IncrementalExecution, a novel online framework that dynamically determines when to stop executing shots based on the principle of point of diminishing returns: the point at which additional shots no longer significantly alter the empirical distribution of a fixed circuit. The framework supports customisable policies for shot management, enabling flexible trade-offs between execution cost and result fidelity within static execution scenarios. We assess our proposal through an extensive experimental evaluation spanning 33,750 framework configurations across 180 unique static quantum circuit-backend combinations, for a total of 7.3M independent experiments. Unlike prior work that relies on problem-specific knowledge or algorithm-dependent assumptions (e.g., variational or adaptive workflows), our approach is applicable to a large set of static circuits and immediately deployable on current quantum cloud platforms.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces an online shot-stopping framework that halts quantum circuit execution when extra shots stop meaningfully changing the empirical output distribution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can cut runtime and cost on noisy quantum hardware by using only the shots needed to reach a target distribution stability for static circuits.
method: IncrementalExecution monitors the evolving empirical distribution after each batch of shots.
It applies a point-of-diminishing-returns stopping rule to decide when to stop.
The framework allows customizable shot-management policies for different cost–fidelity trade-offs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluated 33,750 framework configurations over 180 static circuit-backend combinations, totaling 7.3M independent experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is designed for static black-box circuits, so its stopping policy may need retuning for highly dynamic workflows or when backend conditions drift.
infographic.paper_title: How Many Shots Are Enough for a Quantum Circuit?

title: Quantum solitons and their quantum walks in transmon arrays
authors: Ben Blain, Giampiero Marchegiani, Luigi Amico, Gianluigi Catelani
abstract: Superconducting qubits are artificial atoms whose spectra and interactions can be engineered through appropriate circuit design, a versatility that can be exploited for quantum simulation. We theoretically investigate a linear array of capacitively coupled transmons, effectively described by a Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian with attractive interaction. We revisit the discrete-soliton nature of the lowest-energy band of the spectrum, and identify spatially localized quantum solitons. The solitonic character of these states is revealed through their time evolution, which displays a quantum interference pattern, or quantum walk, highlighting their composite nature. We discuss protocols for preparing spatially localized quantum solitons that are compatible with current state-of-the-art tunable-transmon circuits. Our results demonstrate that superconducting circuits provide a promising and experimentally accessible platform for the investigation of quantum soliton physics.

infographic.key_insight: A line of capacitively coupled transmons can host spatially localized quantum solitons whose dynamics show quantum-walk interference, revealing their composite many-body nature.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work suggests tunable superconducting qubit arrays can be engineered as an experimentally accessible platform for simulating nonlinear quantum transport and soliton physics.
method: Model the transmon chain as an attractive Bose-Hubbard system.
Analyze the lowest-energy band for discrete-soliton states and spatial localization.
Simulate time evolution to expose quantum-walk interference and propose preparation protocols.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical spectral and dynamical analysis showing localized soliton states and their interference patterns, along with protocols compatible with current tunable-transmon circuits.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed solitons and protocols are theoretical, so experimental realization will depend on maintaining sufficient coherence, controllability, and disorder suppression in real transmon arrays.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum solitons and their quantum walks in transmon arrays
